# Design

How this app is built: its stack, layout and conventions.
Read it with `AGENTS.md`, which has the working rules and how the app is tested.

*TanStack's own documentation is vendored in this repo under `docs/tanstack/`: the official
`llms.txt` index for TanStack Router (`router.llms.txt`) and TanStack Query (`query.llms.txt`).
Consult it when working with TanStack Router or Query.*

---

## OfficeFloor REST endpoints — routes MUST live under `rest/api/`

Put every domain REST route under `src/main/resources/officefloor/rest/api/` so its path starts
with `/api/`: `SpaConfig` only lets `/api/*` reach the backend, and a non-`/api/` route is swallowed
by the SPA deep-link fallback (it returns `index.html`, not your endpoint). The reference below uses
non-`/api/` example paths for brevity — in this app the `/api/` prefix is required. See
`src/main/resources/officefloor/README.md`.

---

*The following is OfficeFloor's own agent guidance for this stack, included verbatim
from <https://officefloor.net/AGENTS.md>. It is part of the OfficeFloor architecture.*

## OfficeFloor REST endpoints

Applies when adding or changing REST endpoints. This project serves REST through
OfficeFloor Function Injection, **not** Spring MVC controllers: each endpoint is a
pipeline of small function classes wired together in YAML.

- Requires the OfficeFloor Spring Boot starter in the build:
  `officefloor-rest-spring-boot-4-starter` (Spring Boot 4.x) or
  `officefloor-rest-spring-boot-3-starter` (Spring Boot 3.x). Without it these YAML
  files are inert. (Rules below track these starter versions.)
- Define each endpoint as a YAML file under `src/main/resources/officefloor/rest/`,
  named `<path>.<METHOD>.yml` (e.g. `owners/{ownerId}.PUT.yml` → `PUT /owners/{ownerId}`).
- One small function class per step; compose steps with `next:` and `outputs:`.
- Do NOT generate `@RestController`, `@GetMapping` or `@PostMapping`.

# POST /api/sheets/{sheetId}/claims/{claimId}/status — move a claim to a new status (body
# {status, user, review, reason}): DRAFT to OPEN, OPEN to SETTLED, DRAFT, OPEN or PENDING to VOID,
# and SETTLED to VOID by a steward within 7 days of its settling (its status log's SETTLED date).
# A clerk (any user not assigned steward) settling a claim whose due is above the sheet's clerk limit
# sends it to PENDING instead. A steward reviews a PENDING claim (review true): status SETTLED approves
# it (not by the user who opened it), status OPEN with a reason rejects it. Refused (400) for any
# other change, when the sheet's permission matrix (perm-open, perm-settle, perm-void; by default a
# clerk or a steward) does not allow the user's role to open, settle or void, when settling or approving a claim with no proofs whose due is above the proof threshold
# in force on its date, when opening a claim with an empty note whose due is above the note threshold
# in force on its date (both checked before the clerk limit, so it never goes to PENDING), when the user who opened the claim tries to settle it, when the claim is not on
# the sheet, or when its due-by falls in a closed period; nothing is stored then. Opening records the
# user as the claim's opened-by. A stored change is recorded in the audit file as CLAIM_OPENED,
# CLAIM_PENDING, CLAIM_SETTLED, CLAIM_APPROVED, CLAIM_REJECTED or CLAIM_VOIDED (with reversed=<the
# frozen figure> when a SETTLED claim is voided). While the sheet has void reasons, a void needs one of
# them as its reason (refused otherwise); it is kept on the claim and CLAIM_VOIDED ends with reason=<it>.

content.text:
The change is in, and `bin/e2e` passes all 4 tests in the spec.

Whoever last edited a claim, through the claim form or the row's amount entry, can no longer settle or approve it. As with the opener, the action is refused with an error on the claim and nothing is written. Settling several claims together follows the same rule, because it runs each claim through the same check as a single settle.

**What changed:**
- **Database:** a new migration, `V48__claim_edited_by.sql`, adds an `edited_by` column to `claim` and to its history table `claim_hist`. It drops and recreates the history trigger, as the earlier migrations that added claim columns do.
- **Recording the editor:** `ApplyClaim` now records the user on the claim and `ClaimStore.edit()` saves it. Both kinds of edit go through the same server call, so both record who edited.
- **The check:** `ApplyStatus` now refuses a settle or approve by the user who last edited the claim, with the message "The user who last edited a claim cannot settle/approve it".
- **Docs:** the comments in `status.POST.yml`, `{claimId}.PUT.yml` and `SettleClaims` now describe the new rule.

The front end needed no change, since it already shows a refusal on the claim's error element. No new `data-testid`s or audit records were needed.

Only the latest edit counts: if a second user edits the claim afterwards, the first one can settle it again.
